# The hidden history behind ꜣnpw

Behind the modern ASCII form *anubis* hides a much longer story. **ꜣnpw** reaches back through manuscripts, inscriptions, and oral tradition long before it ever touched a keyboard, and every mark in the restored spelling is a receipt from that journey. In what follows we trace the name from its Hieroglyphs attestations through its mythology, its cult, its symbols, and its afterlife in other cultures — and we show how the PuniCodex project turned that philological record into a Unicode domain that resolves today. The history was never lost. It was only waiting for the infrastructure to catch up.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** ꜣnpw
- **ASCII form:** anubis
- **Meaning:** "Egyptian god of embalming and the necropolis; the name's etymology is uncertain (his epithet tpy-ḏw=f means He who is upon his mountain)"
- **Domain of influence:** Mummification, Afterlife, Jackals
- **Pantheon:** Egyptian
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** 𓃢 (Hieroglyphs)
- **Live domain:** ꜣnpw.com

## Overview

**ꜣnpw** (*anubis*) — He Who Is Upon His Mountain — belongs to the Egyptian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Mummification, Afterlife, Jackals". The name's etymology is uncertain; his epithet tpy-ḏw=f means "He who is upon his mountain".

ꜣnpw is the oldest funeral god of Egypt: lord of the necropolis before Osiris ever ruled it, master of embalming, and the steady hand at the scales where every human heart is weighed against a feather. His black jackal watches from the edge of the desert where the dead were always buried.

PuniCodex restores the name as **ꜣnpw** and serves its temple at [ꜣnpw.com](https://xn--npw-lk3l.com). The restoration preserves a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — the initial alef of the consonantal skeleton — which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *anubis* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Name

The name is attested in Hieroglyphs as **𓃢**. The name's etymology is uncertain; his epithet tpy-ḏw=f means "He who is upon his mountain".

The ASCII form *anubis* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **ꜣnpw** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — the initial alef of the consonantal skeleton — which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **a** → **ꜣ** — Alef ꜣ: glottal stop
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **u** → **p** — P: bilabial stop
- **b** → **—** — Dropped: not in standard
- **i** → **w** — W: bilabial glide
- **s** → **—** — Dropped: final suffix

Attested and derived spellings of the name:

- **Anúbis** — alternate stress, scholarly variant: Acute on upsilon: alternate stress position

The project holds the domain **ꜣnpw.com** (xn--npw-lk3l.com) as the canonical home of this name.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Hieroglyphs as **𓃢** — Egyptian hieroglyphs, attested Egyptian hieroglyphic, c. 3200 BCE – 4th century CE, in Nile Valley, Egypt. The script is written right-to-left / top-to-bottom / multidirectional.

The scholarly transliteration is *ꜣnpw* (Egyptological transliteration), giving the normalized reading Original vocalisation unknown; Egyptological /aː.ˈnuː.bɪs/..

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Recumbent jackal (𓃢) as ideogram and determinative
- Full phonetic spelling can include 𓇋𓈖𓊪𓅱
- God of mummification and guide of the dead

The name is written ꜣ-n-p-w with the recumbent jackal (Gardiner E16) as determinative, over the hotep offering sign in the fuller orthographies. The Greeks heard it as Anoubis; Coptic preserved it as Anoup. The jackal is not decorative: it is the god himself, present in his own spelling.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/jaːˈnaː.paw/** — Egyptological (from ꜣnpw).

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: The name is a consonant skeleton: j-n-p-w; the Greeks vocalized it as Anubis.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Egyptian** — ꜣnpw
- **Greek** — Ἄνουβις
- **Coptic** — Anoup
- **Owned form** — ꜣnpw

Egyptian ꜣnpw is conventionally vocalized "Anupu" or "Anup"; the Greek rendering Anoubis gives English "Anubis." The initial ꜣ (aleph, Gardiner G1) is a glottal consonant Egyptology once ignored and now transcribes — the restoration ꜣnpw keeps the ancient consonantal skeleton exactly as the hieroglyphs write it.

## Mythology

In the earliest religion ꜣnpw simply is the god of the dead; when the Osiris cycle rose, he was written into it — as embalmer, son, and guide — without ever losing his seniority at the grave.

### The First Embalming (The Wrapping)

When Set dismembered Osiris and Isis gathered the pieces, it was ꜣnpw who washed, anointed, and wrapped the god's body — the first mummy, the prototype of every burial thereafter. Egyptian priests performed the rite wearing his jackal mask, and the liturgy addresses the dead as "Osiris," while the hands doing the work are Anubis' own.

### The Feather of Maat (The Judgment)

The Book of the Dead's spell 125 fixes his most famous office: in the Hall of the Two Truths, ꜣnpw leads the deceased before the scales, steadies the beam as the heart is weighed against Maat's feather of truth, and announces the reading to Thoth, who records it. A heart heavy with lies is thrown to Ammit, the devourer — his is the hand that lets that happen, or prevents it.

### Son of Nephthys (The Lineage)

Later tradition (Plutarch's On Isis and the Egyptian sources behind it) makes him the son of Osiris and Nephthys, exposed and raised by Isis — a hidden child of the very murder he would spend eternity repairing. Earlier texts give him humbler parentage, sometimes the cow-goddess Hesat: theologies changed, but his place at the grave never did.

### Opener of the Ways (The Guide)

His title Wp-w3wt — Wepwawet's title too, "Opener of the Ways" — marks his oldest function: the pathfinder through the Duat. On coffins and tomb walls he leans over the bier, one hand on the wrapped body, not as a threat but as the ferryman: no soul reaches the Field of Reeds without his escort through the dark.

### He Who Is Upon His Mountain (The Guide)

His titles mark his oldest functions: jmy-wt, 'He who is in the place of embalming'; ḫnty-jmntjw, 'Foremost of the Westerners'; ḫnty-sḥ-nṯr, 'Foremost of the divine booth'; and tpy-ḏw=f, 'He who is upon his mountain,' the watcher on the necropolis ridge. On coffins and tomb walls he leans over the bier, one hand on the wrapped body, not as a threat but as the ferryman: no soul reaches the Field of Reeds without his escort through the dark.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with ꜣnpw concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **The black jackal** — Black as the fertile Nile silt and the embalmed flesh — the colour of rebirth, not evil
- **The flail** — His authority over the necropolis as its shepherd
- **The scales** — Judgment made precise — his unwavering hand at the beam
- **The imiut fetish** — The headless skin on a pole — the embalmer's ancient emblem, older than his myths

## Archaeology & Evidence

Tutankhamun's tomb (KV62) yielded the Anubis shrine: a life-size black wooden jackal, gilded ears and collar, guarding the canopic equipment — now in Cairo. The Anubeion at Saqqara, excavated over decades, preserves catacombs of mummified dogs and jackals offered to him — estimates run to millions of animals across Egypt's canine catacombs. Vignettes of spell 125, with his hand on the scales, survive in hundreds of Books of the Dead, from the papyrus of Ani in the British Museum to the papyrus of Hunefer.

His great cult centre was **Cynopolis** — 'Dog City' — in Middle Egypt, where the Greeks noted the dogs kept sacred in his temple. The **Anubeion at Saqqara**, excavated beside the Serapeum, preserves his other world: catacombs filled with millions of mummified dogs and jackals, votive offerings of pilgrims from the Late Period to the Roman era. In Greco-Roman Alexandria the temple of **Hermanubis** fused him with Hermês, and Apuleius describes his black-and-gold mask leading the Isiac procession — the Egyptian jackal marching, fully at home, through a Greek city.

## Realm & Domain

ꜣnpw is the oldest funeral god of Egypt: lord of the necropolis before Osiris ever ruled it, master of embalming, and the steady hand at the scales where every human heart is weighed against a feather. His black jackal watches from the edge of the desert where the dead were always buried.

### The Jackal

The desert canid seen at the graves' edge — feared for what it digs, honoured as the grave's defender.

### The Weighing

He steadies the scales in the Hall of Two Truths: heart against Maat's feather, exact to the grain.

### The Embalmer

He wrapped Osiris himself — the first mummy — and every priestly embalmer wore his mask.

### The Psychopomp

"Foremost of the Westerners" — guide of souls through the night roads of the dead.

## Across Cultures

The Greeks, finding a god who guides souls, fused him with Hermês: Hermanubis had temples of his own in Alexandria and Rome, jackal-headed with the kerykeion in hand. Isis' Roman mysteries kept him as mystagogue — Apuleius describes his black-and-gold mask in the Isiac procession at Cenchreae. Early Coptic tradition quietly absorbed him into the psychopomp figure of the archangel Michael, weigher of souls.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[hades|Hádēs]] (underworld / death), [[hermes|Hermês]] (psychopomp), [[kanaloa|Kānāloa]] (underworld / death), [[ker|Kēr]] (underworld / death), [[mot|Mōt]] (underworld / death), and [[persephone|Persephonē]] (underworld / death).

## Cultural Legacy

He is, for most of the world, the face of ancient Egypt: Tutankhamun's black jackal shrine — the recumbent Anubis atop his portable chest — is among the most reproduced objects on earth. Mummification cinema, from Karloff to modern franchises, works his territory; and every modern scale-icon of justice unconsciously borrows the pose of his beam. Egyptologists note the supreme irony: feared as a horror-movie monster, he was antiquity's most trusted guardian.

## A Meditation

ꜣnpw is the god of careful hands. At the two moments a person is most helpless — the body's unmaking and the heart's examination — he is the one who touches gently and reads honestly. Civilizations are judged, the Egyptians believed, by how they treat the dead; he is the god of that judgment, in both senses.

## The Unicode Restoration

ꜣnpw is classified as **Tier 1**: the restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses. The ASCII fallback *anubis* still resolves everywhere, but it is the restored form that carries the name's full information. Across the 6 characters of the name, the restoration adjusts 5: 5 further adjustments (ꜣ, p, b, w, s). That is the whole thesis of this temple: the marks are the message.

## Name Variations

The lexicon records 1 additional form of the name:

- **Anúbis** (alt-stress) — Acute on upsilon: alternate stress position

The temple uses **ꜣnpw** as the primary form: it is the spelling that best balances philological accuracy with the practical limits of DNS.

## The Domain Name

The restored name is live as a working domain: **ꜣnpw.com**, which the DNS carries in punycode form as xn--npw-lk3l.com — an ASCII-compatible encoding that lets a non-ASCII name travel the global network without breaking older infrastructure. The visitor sees ꜣnpw; the machines see the encoding. That duality is the engineering compromise on which the entire restoration rests, and it is why a name written the way its own tradition wrote it in Hieroglyphs can now be typed into any browser on earth.

## Why This Restoration Matters

The story of ꜣnpw did not end in antiquity; it changed medium. Names that survive for millennia do so because each generation finds a new carrier for them — clay, papyrus, print, and now DNS. The PuniCodex restoration simply makes the carrier honest: the spelling that resolves is the spelling the evidence supports. If this post showed anything, it is that *anubis* and **ꜣnpw** are not the same name with different styling. They are a summary and the text it summarizes. The web can now serve the text.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A restored name is a small map. In **ꜣnpw**, the journey from the ASCII fallback *anubis* to the Unicode form can be read letter by letter, and each letter tells a story. Of the 6 characters, 1 remain unchanged; they anchor the name to its modern shape. The remaining adjustments recover marks the source tradition used to distinguish this name from every other word built from the same letters.

The **a** becomes **ꜣ** — Alef ꜣ: glottal stop.

The **n** stays as it is — Same.

The **u** becomes **p** — P: bilabial stop.

The **b** becomes **b** — Dropped: not in standard.

The **i** becomes **w** — W: bilabial glide.

The **s** becomes **s** — Dropped: final suffix.

Together these changes are not decoration. They are the minimum set of marks needed to keep the name legible in its own tradition. Remove them and you still have a string of letters; you no longer have the name as it was written.
